title: Ang 360: the invasion
hook: Guru Nanak's hymn on Babur's invasion
tomorrow: what has to die before something can grow?

segments.voice: Yesterday, ang 349: the light, not caste. Look for the light first, in anyone. Today the same voice looks straight at something very hard to look at.

Something wrong happens right in front of a room, at school, at work, in a group chat, and the room does the usual thing: it changes the subject. Nobody wants to be the one who says it out loud. On ang 360, Guru Nanak is the one who says it. Tradition links this hymn to Babur's invasion of Punjab. And he speaks straight to God, in paraphrase: so much beating, people cried out; did You feel no pain? A gentle note for parents: today's hymn is about violence and grief, told without details.
screen: `THE ROOM CHANGES THE SUBJECT.` → `GURU NANAK DOESN'T.` → `DID YOU FEEL NO PAIN?`

segments.voice: The hymn doesn't use polite words. In paraphrase: the Creator sent the Mughal like death's messenger; there was so much slaughter that people screamed. Then the hard question, aimed upward: did You feel no pain? He goes further. In paraphrase: if one strong man strikes another, no one is troubled; but when a lion falls on a herd, the herd's master must answer for it. Notice what he does. He doesn't pretend it's fine. He doesn't turn it into a quick lesson about patience. He names who did it and what it cost, and he takes the complaint right to the top. A hymn can argue with God out loud and still be a hymn. This one sits in the scripture Sikhs bow to, complaint and all. That's what this page gives an ordinary week. When something is wrong, the first honest thing isn't to make it sound smaller. It's to name it: what happened, who was hurt, and that it mattered.
screen: `NO POLITE WORDS.` · `DID YOU FEEL NO PAIN?` · `THE LION AND THE HERD.` · `NAME WHAT HAPPENED AND WHO IT HURT.` · then, large: `HE NAMED IT.`

segments.voice: Read ang 360 if you can, slowly, aloud or in a whisper. Then say one quiet sentence out loud about something wrong you've seen lately: what happened, and who it hurt. No fixing it yet. Let the rest of the sit be the stillness after a true sentence.
Ang 360. The page of Guru Nanak's Asa hymn that names the invasion and asks God: did You feel no pain?
Pocket this: he named it, the harm and the hurt, out loud and all the way up. Go gently.

howItsDone: Guru Nanak's hymns on the invasion, which Sikhs call Babarvani, are read in order in Raag Asa and sung as kirtan; Sikhs remember them as the Guru speaking up for people who suffered.

notes: 2026-10-15 v3 written: shape life (a situation from this week: the room that changes the subject; what the hymn gives you for it: name it).
Hard scene: the hymn speaks of slaughter. One gentle line for parents is in the hook; no graphic detail is given.

Ang 360 lines paraphrased: the Creator sent the Mughal as death's messenger (jam kar mugal charaaiaa); so much beating that people cried out, did You feel no pain? (etee maar paee karlaane tain kee darad na aaiaa); the strong-on-strong vs lion-on-herd line. Confirm Ang and senses.

'Tradition links this hymn to Babur's invasion of Punjab': hedged; the hymn names the Mughal and Khurasan, not Babur by name. The term Babarvani is used in howItsDone and the trapdoor as the name Sikhs give these hymns; confirm.
The application ('the first honest thing is to name it') is the lesson's reading, framed for an ordinary week; it does not equate small wrongs with the invasion.
v3 storyline: Simran tells her dad Harjit about taya ji's question; he says 'not before the wedding.' She is weighing whether to stay quiet. Pacing: no confrontation today.
